dashboard.title: Redis
dashboard.description: Monitor a self-hosted Redis instance: rejected connections, evictions, cache hit rate, memory use, throughput, and replication.

visuals.title: Rejected connections
visuals.description: Connections refused because the maxclients limit was reached. Any sustained value here means clients are being turned away: raise maxclients or reduce the size of your connection pools.

visuals.title: Evicted keys
visuals.description: Keys removed because Redis reached its maxmemory limit. Evictions mean silent data loss: dropped cache entries, and dropped jobs when Redis backs a queue. Investigate memory growth or raise maxmemory.

visuals.title: Blocked clients
visuals.description: Clients waiting on a blocking call such as BLPOP. A steady count is normal for queue workers, but a rising count means consumers are not keeping up with producers.

visuals.title: Keyspace hits vs misses
visuals.description: Successful and failed key lookups in the main dictionary. A rising share of misses means cached data is expiring or being evicted before it gets read, which pushes load onto your database.

visuals.title: Expired keys
visuals.description: Keys removed because their TTL elapsed. Unlike evictions this is healthy, expected behaviour, but a sudden change in shape often explains a drop in cache hit rate.

visuals.title: Memory used
visuals.description: Memory allocated by Redis as seen by its own allocator (used), by the operating system (RSS), and the highest value reached since startup (peak). Used memory approaching your maxmemory limit is what precedes evictions.

visuals.title: Memory fragmentation ratio
visuals.description: Ratio between memory the operating system reserved (RSS) and memory Redis allocated. Around 1.0 is healthy. Above 1.5 means fragmentation is wasting memory; below 1.0 means Redis has been swapped to disk and latency will suffer.

visuals.title: Commands processed
visuals.description: Total commands handled by the server. Read this alongside memory and network throughput to judge whether the instance is saturated.

visuals.title: Commands per second
visuals.description: Commands processed per second, as Redis reports it. This is the throughput figure to compare against latency and memory when judging whether the instance is saturated.

visuals.title: Network throughput
visuals.description: Bytes read from and written to the network. Large output volumes usually point at oversized values or commands such as KEYS and HGETALL returning more data than callers need.

visuals.title: Connected clients
visuals.description: Client connections currently open, excluding replicas. Compare against your maxclients limit: a count climbing towards it is what produces rejected connections.

visuals.title: Connections received
visuals.description: Connections accepted since startup. A high rate against a flat connected-client count means clients are reconnecting for every operation instead of pooling, which wastes round trips.

visuals.title: Keyspace size per database
visuals.description: Keys held per database, and how many of them carry an expiration. Keys without a TTL accumulate indefinitely and are a common cause of gradual memory growth.

visuals.title: Connected replicas
visuals.description: Replicas currently connected to this instance. A drop to zero on a primary means replication has broken and you have no standby to fail over to.

visuals.title: Changes since last save
visuals.description: Writes accumulated since the last successful RDB snapshot. A number that keeps climbing without resetting means persistence is failing, and a restart would lose everything since the last save.
